title: Contextual Economy - kitchen scraps and experiment ideas
content:
Quick scatter of ideas and reading takeaways about the cost/latency tradeoffs from long contexts — intended as a labbook I can grab from when sketching an experiment or PR: 

Top papers/blogs skimmed (very quick notes):
- "Attention is All You Need" (Vaswani et al.) — reminder: self-attention cost O(n^2), so anything beyond ~8k tokens needs architectural work or smart caching. Notes: revisit decoder-only optimizations and sparse attention variants.
- "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" — qualitative takeaway: marginal utility of extra context vs compute isn't linear; for some tasks adding more context is diminishing returns unless retrieval is targeted.
- "KV-Cache Compression" (recent arXiv) — promising lossy compression of KV states reduces memory by ~3x with small downstream quality drop on recency tasks. Worth re-running on our quantized runtimes.
- Blog: "Prefix caching is a hack but useful" — practical rules: 1) cache at token-block boundaries, 2) expire based on semantic novelty, not just time.

Short takeaways (what surprised me):
1) Small eviction heuristics based on token-level surprisal outperform simple LRU for dialog streams with repetitive system prompts.
2) Batching + small cache-window improves tail latency more than naive batching when requests have high prefix overlap.
3) Quantized runtimes magnify sensitivity to compression noise; need quality probes tied to prompt archetypes.

Experiment ideas to run in short sprints (priority order):
A) "Surprisal-driven eviction" pilot: instrument a hosted model route, compute token surprisal for incoming prefixes (cheap approximation), evict KV-cache entries with low surprisal contribution. Metric: avg latency, 95th pct latency, prompt-quality delta (ROUGE/embedding-sim) on curated recency set.
B) "Block-compressed cache for 8k->32k" prototype: adapt existing low-bit storage format to store KV blocks and add a lightweight decompression on miss. Measure memory breakdown and decode latency.
C) "Semantic novelties as expiry" A/B vs TTL: maintain an embedding fingerprint for cached prefixes; when new prefix embedding distance > threshold, force partial refresh. Track token cost and coherence on long-form summarization tasks.

Quick prompt tests I ran (notes):
- Test: repeat system prompt 5x, then ask for doc-specific answer. With LRU evict, model forgot earlier doc sections at ~7k tokens; with surprisal-evict, recall maintained longer.
- Test: small-block compression + 4-bit quantized runtime introduced occasional token duplication on beam-like continuations — needs guard.

Open questions / unknowns (for follow-up):
- How much of observed quality degradation is due to kernel quantization vs block compression algorithm? Need an isolating matrix of experiments.
- Are there cheap embedding-distance approximations (hashing) that are robust enough to trigger semantic expiry without adding heavy CPU?
- Can we piggyback cache pruning on existing routing events to make it near-zero-cost?

Immediate next actions (this week):
- Draft a short experiment plan for A) and sync with Maya for instrumentation (JIRA:INF-921).
- Short spike to port block-compression proof-of-concept from research repo (GH: redwood/context-cache#67) into a microservice and measure decode p50/p95.
- Add 20 prompt archetypes to the lightweight eval harness (include summarization, Q&A over long doc, multi-turn chat).

Notes to self: keep this doc informal. If an idea looks good, I will copy a cleaned version into a formal PR description or a Confluence brief.
